title: Walking meditation
hookLine: slow walking, feeling each step, as taught in Buddhist monasteries

lines: A MONK ON A SHORT PATH.
cards: Early morning, a monastery courtyard in Thailand or Myanmar. A monk walks a straight path of maybe twenty paces. At the end, he stops, turns slowly, and walks back.
Then again. And again. For an hour.

He isn't going anywhere, and that's the point. Most walking is getting from here to there: to the car, to the fridge, to the next thing, with the mind already arrived. This kind has nowhere to arrive.
Every step is the whole trip. Yesterday's walk was for thinking. Today's is for not thinking.

teach.b: In the Pali texts, the word for it is cankama, walking up and down, and the walking path itself carries the same name.
In one short teaching from the book of fives, the Buddha lists five benefits of walking meditation. It gives you endurance for journeys. It gives you endurance for effort.
It's good for health. It helps digestion. And the calm you find while walking lasts a long time.
That last one matters: a calm that can walk is a calm you can take into the day. The practice looks different from school to school.
In Burmese vipassana, taught by teachers like Mahasi Sayadaw, you break each step into parts and note them silently: lifting, moving, placing.
In Zen, kinhin is walking meditation between long sits, slow, hands held at the chest, one half step to each breath.

In the twentieth century, the Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught walking meditation to large groups, often outdoors, in Asia, Europe and North America. The common thread is simple. Feel the foot.
Feel the weight shift. Let the next step be the only step.
When your mind drifts to the grocery list, and it will, you notice, and come back to the sole of your foot.
It's the same move as watching the breath, done with legs.

how: In Buddhist monasteries of several schools, monks and visitors alternate sitting meditation with walking meditation on a short straight path, walking slowly and turning at each end.

a race walked against the clock
slow, mindful steps on a short path

s: walking meditation is about getting somewhere calmly
there's nowhere to arrive: a short path, turn, and walk back.
the Buddha lists five benefits of walking meditation
endurance for journeys and effort, health, digestion, and a calm that lasts.
when your mind drifts, the practice has failed
you notice, and come back to the sole of your foot. that is the practice.

games.q: you're a monk at the end of your twenty-pace path. what now?
o: speed up to get more steps in.
games.why: you turn, slowly, and walk back, again and again. the path goes nowhere, so every step is the whole trip.

practice: Stand if you can; if not, keep your feet on the floor where you sit. Shift your weight into one foot, then lift, move and place the other, feeling the heel, then the whole sole, take the weight, and say inside: this step.
Take ten steps slower than feels normal, and if you run out of room, turn slowly and come back.

wordCard.voice: Walking meditation. Slow steps on a short path, feeling each one, as taught in Buddhist monasteries. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, cankama (caṅkama): walking up and down; the word also names the walking path itself.

carryVoice: Your line: this step. Every step is the whole trip. One hundred thirty days now.
